explanations.explanation: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, writes that these exiles were "…sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ…" (1 Peter 1:2). Look at who shows up in that one verse: God the Father, the Spirit and Jesus Christ. Peter puts all three right there in his greeting. Good work, friend.

Peter doesn't name any elders in this verse. He says these exiles were "…sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ…" (1 Peter 1:2). I know, an elder sounds like a safe guess, like grabbing the nearest cookie off the cooling rack. This one belongs to the Spirit.

Priests never come up in this verse. Peter says these exiles were "…sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ…" (1 Peter 1:2). It's the Spirit doing the sanctifying, and Peter puts it right next to God the Father's foreknowledge. Easy mix-up, friend, so keep the Spirit in mind.

That's it. Peter says God "…has given us new birth into a living hope…" (1 Peter 1:3). Not a dead hope, not a maybe-someday hope, a LIVING one. And he says it comes by God's great mercy, so nobody has to earn it with a perfect batch.

Close to something that sounds churchy, but that's not what Peter says here. In this verse, the new birth is "…into a living hope…" (1 Peter 1:3). He also says it comes by God's great mercy. Hang on to that living hope, friend.

A quiet rest does sound nice, friend. I could use one after a double batch. But Peter says the new birth is "…into a living hope…" (1 Peter 1:3). Hope that's alive, and it's tied to Jesus rising from the dead.

Yes, the resurrection. Peter says the living hope comes "…through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead…" (1 Peter 1:3). The hope is alive because Jesus is risen. That's the whole reason the oven stays on in my bakery.

Baptism is a real thing in Scripture, but it's not the word in this verse. Peter says the living hope comes "…through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead…" (1 Peter 1:3). The hope is tied to Jesus rising. Put that word right back in the blank, friend.

Teaching is good stuff, and I do plenty of it. But Peter's word here is resurrection. He says the living hope comes "…through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead…" (1 Peter 1:3). Jesus rising from the dead is what makes that hope alive.

Careful, friend, because Peter says the opposite. He calls the inheritance "…imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you…" (1 Peter 1:4). Unfading means it does not slowly fade. That inheritance is kept safe in heaven.

False is right. Peter says the inheritance is "…imperishable, undefiled, and unfading…" (1 Peter 1:4). It doesn't spoil, it doesn't get stained, and it doesn't fade. And it's reserved in heaven for them, so it's already put away safe.

Power is the word. Peter says these believers "…are shielded by God’s power…" (1 Peter 1:5). Shielded, friend. That's not me holding the oven door shut with my mustache, that's God's own power doing the guarding.

Law is a fair guess, but it's not what Peter writes. He says these believers "…are shielded by God’s power…" (1 Peter 1:5). The shield is God's power, and it works through faith. Slide that word into the blank.

A temple is a big building, and Peter isn't talking about a building here. He says these believers "…are shielded by God’s power…" (1 Peter 1:5). God's power is the shield, friend. Nothing made of stone.

True. Peter says gold "…perishes even though refined by fire…" (1 Peter 1:7). Gold goes through the fire and still perishes. And he says the proven character of their faith is more precious than that. I'd take that trade any day of the week.

Peter really does say it. He says their proven faith is "…more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire…" (1 Peter 1:7). Gold is shiny, but he says it perishes anyway. Their faith is worth more than that.

explanations.answer: At the revelation of Jesus Christ
explanations.explanation: Right on time. Peter says their proven faith "…may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ." (1 Peter 1:7). He points to that moment, not to some earlier finish line. And he never says when that is, so I keep my ovens ready.

explanations.answer: At the end of their exile in Pontus
explanations.explanation: Pontus is one of the places Peter names in his greeting, but it isn't the answer. He says their proven faith "…may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ." (1 Peter 1:7). The moment he points to is Jesus being revealed. Peter doesn't say anything about their exile ending.

explanations.answer: At the gathering of all the churches
explanations.explanation: A big church gathering would be a great potluck, but that's not in this verse. Peter says their proven faith "…may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ." (1 Peter 1:7). The moment is the revelation of Jesus Christ. Nothing else gets named.

True. Peter writes, "Though you have not seen Him, you love Him…" (1 Peter 1:8). They've never laid eyes on Jesus, and they love Him anyway. They also believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy.

Peter says the opposite. He writes, "Though you have not seen Him, you love Him…" (1 Peter 1:8). Not seeing Him didn't stop the love. He adds that they believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy.
Salvation, yes. Peter says they are "…receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls." (1 Peter 1:9). That's the goal, friend, the finished box. And he says they're receiving it now.

Judgment is not what Peter hands them. He says they are "…receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls." (1 Peter 1:9). The goal of their faith is salvation. Pop that word in the blank.

Testing does show up in the passage, since Peter talks about trials in verse 6. But the goal of their faith is something else. He says they are "…receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls." (1 Peter 1:9). The trials are on the way, and the goal is salvation.

explanations.answer: His sufferings and the glories to follow
explanations.explanation: You nailed it. Peter says the Spirit of Christ in the prophets "…predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow." (1 Peter 1:11). Sufferings first, glories after. I think that order is worth slowing down for.

explanations.answer: His birth and His baptism in the river
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't list those here. He says the Spirit of Christ in the prophets "…predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow." (1 Peter 1:11). Two things, friend: the sufferings, then the glories. Birth and baptism aren't in that verse.

explanations.answer: His kingdom and the temple He would build
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't mention a temple here. He says the Spirit of Christ in the prophets "…predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow." (1 Peter 1:11). Those are the two things. Stick with the sufferings and the glories.

Yes, them. Peter says it was revealed to the prophets "…that they were not serving themselves, but you…" (1 Peter 1:12). The "you" is the folks reading his letter. Those prophets searched and investigated carefully, and they were serving Peter's readers all along. I feel that in my mustache.

Kings are a fair guess, but Peter doesn't say that. He says it was revealed to the prophets "…that they were not serving themselves, but you…" (1 Peter 1:12). The "you" is the people reading his letter. They're the ones being served.
Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. Peter says it was revealed to the prophets "…that they were not serving themselves, but you…" (1 Peter 1:12). That "you" means the people reading his letter.

True. The last line of the passage says, "Even angels long to look into these things." (1 Peter 1:12). Angels, friend. Peter says they long to look into the very things the gospel preachers announced. I think that makes the good news pretty special.

Peter does say it. The last line of the passage is, "Even angels long to look into these things." (1 Peter 1:12). Angels long to look into the very things the gospel preachers announced. That's a pretty big crowd leaning in.
